newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin ready to play Belarus card in NATO contest.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin ready to play Belarus card in NATO contest.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, coming back from a long illness to battle NATO's eastward encroachment, will revive talks on uniting with western neighbour Belarus when President Alexander Lukashenko visits Moscow on Friday.

Yeltsin, who first raised the prospect of extending Moscow's direct influence back to the Polish frontier a year ago, is expected to float the idea of joint referendums on the move in a keynote speech to the Russian parliament on Thursday.
The West could be troubled by such a union, which due to the vast difference in size between the two former Soviet states would leave Moscow calling the shots.

Belarus's neighbours in Poland and the Baltic states, whose painful memories of Soviet domination have fuelled their demands for NATO membership, would be concerned. To the south, Ukraine, which has frosty relations with Moscow, may also disapprove.

On April 2 last year, pre-empting his communist challenger's call to start restoring the Soviet Union, Yeltsin signed a pact with Lukashenko which formed an economic community and opened the way for developing political ties between Moscow and Minsk.

Since winning re-election in July, however, Yeltsin has been largely out of action with heart trouble and then pneumonia. Ties with Belarus languished, not helped by last autumn's crisis in Minsk, which saw Russian mediators looking embarrassed and ineffectual as Lukashenko swept aside parliamentary opposition.
But this week has marked a major step in the 66-year-old Yeltsin's political comeback and he has already indicated that the Belarus question is back on the Kremlin's agenda.
He told a visiting European Union delegation on Monday the EU should take a "more constructive approach" to Belarus and said Russian-Belarussian integration had a lot further to go.

Interfax news agency reported last week that Yeltsin and Lukashenko had agreed in principle to hold simultaneous national referendums on closer integration, and that Yeltsin would mention it in Thursday's state of the nation address in parliament.

Yeltsin first raised the idea of a referendum on integration in a letter to Lukashenko in January. He outlined a possible single government with unified tax laws, economic reforms and, crucially for fuel-starved Belarus, a common energy system.

Beneath an authoritarian manner, Lukashenko, 42, enjoys solid support among Belarus's 10 million people. He stresses their common Slav heritage with Russia and makes a point of speaking in Russian rather than its close cousin Belarussian.
The course of integration is, however, unlikely to run completely smoothly. Unlike Russia, Belarus is criticised by international lenders for failing to reform its Soviet-era planned economy.
On Tuesday, Lukashenko's Prime Minister Sergei Ling said: "Integration with Russia remains a top priority, but we will take our own path to the market economy."

Despite such potential conflicts, diplomats say new talk of unity gives Russia a potent weapon in its fight to block NATO's plans to invite Poland and other former Warsaw Pact states in eastern Europe to join the alliance as early as this summer.
Lukashenko, who once called NATO a "monster", called on Tuesday for a Belarus-NATO treaty, echoing Russia's approach.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright last month proposed a "sensitive region" in eastern Europe to include Belarus where military ground equipment could not be increased.
Privately, U.S. officials say they are unsure how to respond if Russia-Belarus integration efforts go forward.

Many Russians, nostalgic for the days of the Soviet superpower, welcome the idea of union with Belarus. Lukashenko was voted most popular foreign politician in an opinion poll in December. He could become a serious player in Moscow politics.
But other Russians wonder if Belarus might be an economic liability for taxpayers among Russia's 150 million population.

Sixty percent of Minsk residents back integration, a recent poll showed. Among typical answers, one Belarussian said: "I am for a single state with one dicatator-president. Russian resources and our brains can strengthen the economy."
